title: The ordinary
hookLine: a monk at the kitchen sink and a Zen saying about carrying water: awe needs no mountain

cards: By his own account, he never much liked kitchen work. That's where he was put anyway: pots stacked high, a fire that needs feeding, a crowd of hungry brothers about to arrive.
His name was Brother Lawrence, a lay brother in a Carmelite house in Paris. He wasn't a well-known preacher or a scholar. He cooked, and later he mended sandals.

Yet people came to ask him about prayer, and his friends kept his letters and wrote down his conversations. What they kept is a small book about one surprising claim: the kitchen was as holy as the chapel.

teach.h: THE KITCHEN AS HOLY AS THE CHAPEL.
teach.b: First, the kitchen. In the conversations his friends recorded, Brother Lawrence says the time of work was no different, for him, from the time of prayer.
In the noise and clatter of the kitchen, with several people calling for different things at once, he said he held God in as much calm as if he were on his knees at the altar.
He even turned an omelet, so the account goes, for the love of God. He wasn't escaping the chores to find God somewhere else. Second, the practice behind it.

teach.h: COME BACK, MANY SMALL TIMES A DAY.
teach.b: He called it the practice of the presence of God: a simple, steady turning of attention, many small times a day, back toward God while the hands kept working. When he forgot, he said, he didn't punish himself.
He just came back. Third, a neighbor from a very different place.
In Zen Buddhism there's an old saying, credited by tradition to a lay Buddhist named Pang, that the marvelous power he'd found was carrying water and chopping wood.
No visions, no miracles: the water and the wood, done awake.

teach.h: THE SACRED IS WHERE THE WORK IS.
teach.b: Fourth, where the two meet and part. Brother Lawrence was a Catholic Christian, and the presence he turned toward was God.
The Zen saying points to wakefulness, seeing what's in front of you fully, with no God named. They're not saying the same thing, and neither needs the other.
But both put the sacred in the same unlikely spot: right where the work is.

how: Some Christians read Brother Lawrence's The Practice of the Presence of God and try to turn their attention to God during daily work; in Zen monasteries, cooking, cleaning and other chores are treated as part of practice.

o: a plain life with nothing in it worth a second look
plain chores where a cook and a Zen saying found wonder
the dull parts of life that faith tells you to escape

games.q: you're Brother Lawrence. the kitchen is loud, everyone wants something at once, and it's time to pray. what do you do?
o: leave the pots and hurry to the chapel.
stay at the stove and pray right there, as calmly as on your knees.
wait until the work is done and pray then.
games.why: he said the time of work was no different from the time of prayer: in the clatter of the kitchen he held God as calmly as at the altar.

practice: Choose one chore, washing a cup, folding a shirt, wiping a counter, and walk through it slowly in your mind: the weight of the thing, the temperature of the water, the sound it makes.
If you pray, turn toward God as your hands work, the way Brother Lawrence did; if you don't, let the chore be fully seen for once.

wordCard.voice: The ordinary. The pots, the water, the wood: where a Carmelite cook and a Zen saying both found something worth wondering at. Today's word.

orig.note: French: the presence of God, from the title of the small book of Brother Lawrence's conversations and letters.

carryVoice: Your line: awe in the ordinary. Sometimes the vast thing is hiding in a sink full of plates. Rest well.
